title: Union Pier / A softer harbour edge
subtitle: An urban design narrative and review system informed by David Sim’s Soft City
method: Nine project-specific checks adapted from Soft City themes. They are not a code, a scored certification or an engineering feasibility approval. Published author excerpts were consulted; this document does not claim a complete reading of the book.
narrative: A neighbourhood opens gradually to its harbour: familiar streets lead to shared gardens, gardens rise into a local market, and the market releases into an open timber pier. Density belongs where it can sustain everyday services; the waterfront belongs to public life.

chapters.title: Belong to Charleston
chapters.text: Union Pier begins with the streets around it. Ansonborough informs the western sequence of brick, piazza and garden; the southern quarter draws on the passages and layered commercial life of the French Quarter. Contemporary civic buildings give the new district its own addresses and skyline.
chapters.test: Compare block size, entrances, heights and walking connections on the same mapped extent. Keep archived uses distinct from verified current occupation.

chapters.title: Make density useful
chapters.text: Useful density brings homes, work and everyday services together. Fine-grained residential frontages enclose shared courts. Sculpted cultural buildings, terraced hotels and a daylit museum establish distinct public addresses, with generous entrances at the scale of the street.
chapters.test: Measure building footprints and storeys; then schedule homes, local shops, community uses and tenure. A floor-area proxy is not a population or affordability result.

chapters.title: Choose how to walk
chapters.text: A direct route makes daily trips legible. Alongside it, curved garden walks reveal successive trees, courts and glimpses of the harbour. The invitation to linger comes from changing spaces and useful destinations; people can always choose a clear, shorter way through.
chapters.test: Trace continuous step-free routes, crossings, gradients, clear widths and detour ratios. Test the route from the perspective of a child, older resident, wheelchair user and delivery worker.

chapters.title: Trade beneath a shared roof
chapters.text: The market is a family of iron-and-glass halls: six larger garden halls and twelve smaller, individually rotated halls clustered towards the pier. La Boqueria informs the exposed trusses, coloured entrance glazing and visible stalls. Translucent roofs sit over open aisles; garden paths reach all eighteen halls. The heavier programme remains inside the Battery interface, with a public pier beyond.
chapters.test: Confirm daily-service tenancy, loading hours, waste routes, servicing clearances and separation from the busiest pedestrian crossings.

chapters.title: Open the edge to ordinary life
chapters.text: Beyond the heavier landward buildings, a timber pier on piles becomes a sequence of open rooms: shaded pavilions, activity courts, fishing and viewing terraces, and five harbour cutouts. Rain courts change the experience after a storm. The public edge welcomes residents as well as visitors.
chapters.test: Check shade, wind, marine durability, pile loads, guards, rescue access, drainage and the distinction between rain storage and tidal water. No swimming or boat-access programme is implied.

chapters.title: Let the district change
chapters.text: The plan needs an operating life as well as a physical form. Shared courts can host small events; open pavilions accommodate changing uses. Local tenancy, public access, maintenance and ecological care become design decisions with named responsibilities, rather than promises attached to a rendering.
chapters.test: Prepare a public-access covenant, tenancy and maintenance brief, planting strategy and phased delivery plan before claiming social or environmental performance.

checks.question: Does density create useful proximity without a monotonous street wall?
checks.move: Retain residential address rhythms and differentiate six civic, hotel and port landmarks with sculpted roof forms and terraces.
checks.evidence: 189 retained district bodies, six landmark bodies and eighteen covered market halls. The pier-facing row doubles from six to twelve smaller halls.
checks.measure: Footprint, storeys, frontage length, entrance spacing, ground-floor use mix.
checks.next: Confirm entrance locations, household mix and ground-floor tenancy.

checks.question: Can people find different spaces for quiet, play, meeting and looking out?
checks.move: Two major lawns, shared courts, heritage forecourt, market courts, five harbour cutouts, two activity courts and six shade pavilions.
checks.evidence: Five cutouts and two sports surfaces are explicit geometry; sports markings are conceptual, not regulation certification.
checks.status: Modelled / use and comfort to test
checks.measure: Accessible public area by use, seating choices, step-free reach and overlapping activities.
checks.next: Add seating schedules and test noisy/quiet adjacencies.

checks.question: Can buildings and public spaces adapt through a day and over years?
checks.move: Open market halls with visible stalls, partial rear-row mezzanines and independent roof frames offer different occupation scales. Open pier pavilions remain available for public activity.
checks.evidence: Stall counters, roof frames and concept mezzanines are modelled. Trader leases, fit-out services, structure and escape arrangements are unresolved.
checks.measure: Structural bay, service zone, subdivisibility, servicing and occupation schedule.
checks.next: Draw one typical hall plan and one event-day operating plan.

checks.question: Does a person encounter a door, shade and a place to pause rather than a blank edge?
checks.move: Charleston galleries meet expressive civic entrances, open market aisles and transparent pitched roofs.
checks.evidence: Thirty market entrance connections are explicit geometry; residential door and seating schedules remain to develop.
checks.measure: Active frontage ratio, doors per 100 m, canopy depth, seating and overlooking.
checks.next: Develop representative street sections and an entrance inventory.

checks.theme: A direct walk and a slower choice
checks.question: Can everyone understand and complete the route without being forced into a detour?
checks.move: Keep direct contour walks; add garden meanders, pier loops and four broad crossings. Route one service lane smoothly onto the pier.
checks.evidence: Eighteen halls connect to the garden walk through thirty entrance paths. Sampled branch centreline grades stay below 4.58%; the service road remains about 454 m long, 4.2 m wide and at most 2.65% on its sampled centreline. Crossfall and whole-route continuity are not yet certified.
checks.measure: Route connectivity, length/direct distance, running and cross slopes, crossings, headroom and vehicle swept paths.
checks.next: Audit the complete step-free network and track the nominated emergency/service vehicles.

checks.question: Can residents recognise their addresses and use the waterfront without becoming customers?
checks.move: Retain the Bennett Rice Mill facade; connect it to a contemporary gateway and public parks. Keep the waterfront route outside ticketed or commercial premises.
checks.evidence: Heritage and new gateway are modelled; public-access rights and affordable tenancy are not established.
checks.measure: Public/private edge map, opening hours, tenure, affordable space and resident feedback.
checks.next: Create an ownership/access brief and local-business allocation strategy.

checks.question: Is outdoor life comfortable in summer sun, rain and harbour winds?
checks.move: Combine tree canopies, galleries and six open pier shade roofs; offer sheltered and exposed spaces.
checks.evidence: The current roofs, massing and tree locations supersede revision D ray-test percentages. Transparent glazing cannot be treated as opaque shade.
checks.measure: Hourly occupied-area shade, seasonal solar access, wind exposure and thermal comfort.
checks.next: Rerun solar and comfort tests on revision G, including glazing transmission, glare, shading and ventilation.

checks.question: Can the urban layout reduce material and travel demand?
checks.move: Keep heavier bazaar buildings landward, limit enclosed pier mass, reuse a consistent material family and connect everyday uses on foot.
checks.evidence: Material names are coordinated; there is no embodied-carbon calculation or verified modal shift.
checks.measure: Material quantities, reuse potential, lifecycle carbon, maintenance cycles and trip patterns.
checks.next: Quantify the pile/deck/parking structure and compare alternatives before claiming carbon savings.

checks.question: Does the landscape support habitat and manage rain as a connected system?
checks.move: Link the two lawns with a planted rise; add varied garden spaces and keep rain courts distinct from harbour cutouts.
checks.evidence: Tree instances and terrain are schematic. Species diversity, soil volumes, runoff and floodwall performance are not resolved.
checks.status: Geometry present / ecology and hydraulics open
checks.measure: Canopy cover, species and habitat diversity, rooting volume, runoff balance, water quality and flood continuity.
checks.next: Develop planting and drainage sections with ecological and coastal specialists.

review_cycle: Observe the context and state the evidence date.
Describe the everyday experience the design should support.
Draw the spatial move in the current model.
Measure geometry; test programme and operations separately.
Record what is demonstrated, conditional or still untested.
Revise the model and regenerate every dependent drawing.
decision: Proceed with the urban-design study. Do not describe flood protection, structural capacity, fire access, accessibility, carbon or commercial viability as proven.
precedent_note: Original academic design informed by the named precedents. Studio Gang and Steven Holl Architects did not design or endorse this proposal. La Boqueria is interpreted through the supplied image and official heritage documentation.
